newsitem.title: CANADA: Thai effort to extradite banker suffers more delays.
newsitem.headline: Thai effort to extradite banker suffers more delays.

text.p: Thailand was dealt another delay on Monday in its effort to extradite a former bank official from Canada to face charges of defrauding the ailing Bangkok Bank of Commerce.
An extradition hearing against Rakesh Saxena, former treasury advisor to the bank, was due to begin on Monday in British Columbia Supreme Court after being put off last autumn.
But at the start of the proceeding, Saxena's lawyer applied to have the banker's original arrest warrant quashed, a procedural challenge that made it unclear when extradition proceedings could begin.

Canadian and Thai police arrested Saxena last July at the Whistler ski resort near Vancouver. An Indian citizen and former resident of Thailand, Saxena is accused of colluding with a group of Bangkok Bank of Commerce executives to embezzle about $65 million.
The Thai government took over the bank a year ago after a public run on deposits sparked by news it was saddled with about $2.7 billion in bad loans.

The run on deposits was triggered by opposition party charges about the bad loans and the case took on political overtones. Since Saxena's arrest, he has been named in a second similar case along with Saudi tycoon Adnan Khashoggi.
Canadian government lawyers, who are representing Thailand in the case, said on Monday they would immediately seek a new arrest warrant if the original one were quashed.
Saxena's lawyer, Winton Derby, told the Justice Frank Maczko that he would appeal any decision that went against Saxena and apply to have the extradition hearing postponed.

Saxena appeared briefly in court on Monday but left when it became clear the extradition hearing would not get underway. He was required last year to surrender his passport, post bail of C$1.25 million ($926,000), stay within the Vancouver area and report daily to police.

Since then, he has been living in Vancouver and tending to his business interests from a local office. He has also launched a legal counterattack by lodging defamation lawsuits in Canada against Thai government officials and media outlets.

In Monday's proceeding, Saxena's lawyer argued that the original arrest warrant against Saxena was improperly issued because no prosecution against him had been launched in Thailand at the time. He said this meant the warrant did not meet the requirements of extradition treaties.

Deborah Strachan, the lawyer representing Thailand, disagreed, saying the requirements of the extradition treaty were met because a valid Thai arrest warrant was outstanding. Since then, prosecution has begun in Thailand so a new arrest warrant could immediately be sought if necessary, she said.
Arguments on the matter were set to continue until later in the week.
